659.title: As the Word comes to me, Lalo
659.word: As the Word comes to me
659.hook: as the Lord's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo (Tilang M1, ang 722)
659.tomorrow: The one whose head He guards
659.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Tilang shabad addressed to Bhai Lalo, one of the hymns known as the Babar Vani, and cite its opening line as a model of fearless, truthful speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, whatever you ask, and your line: ask your master. What good thing did you ask for? Today the asking stops, and Guru Nanak speaks hard truth to an old friend. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Early in the path, we met Bhai Lalo, the carpenter of Saidpur, whose plain bread Guru Nanak chose over a rich man's feast. Later, tradition says, the same town was sacked by Babur's army, come down from Kabul, and Guru Nanak was there and was taken captive for a time. Afterward he sang about what he'd seen. And he addressed the song not to a king, and not to the crowd, but to his friend, the carpenter.
screen: `LALO, THE CARPENTER OF SAIDPUR.` → `THE SAME TOWN IS SACKED.` → `A SONG TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Tilang, on ang 722. It opens, in effect: as the Master's Word comes to me, so I speak, Lalo. Then it describes the invasion with terrible clarity. The invader came from Kabul like a wedding party of sin, demanding a bride by force. Modesty and righteousness hid themselves; falsehood strutted about as leader. The religious officials of both communities, the qazis and the brahmins, were pushed aside. And the women, the hymn says, women of every community, suffered. Songs of blood were being sung. Two things stand out. First, the courage of it. Guru Nanak names an invader's violence plainly, while that power was rising over Punjab. He doesn't soften it or flatter it. He says what he saw. Second, why he can. The first line is the key: as the Word comes to me, so I speak. The word is baani, the same word that's in Gurbani, the Guru's word. Guru Nanak isn't offering his own opinion about politics. He's saying the Word moves through him, and he won't edit it to keep himself safe. The line is often quoted as a standard for honest speech: say what is true, as it comes, even to power. And notice who he tells it to. Not the emperor's court. Lalo, a working man, a friend. Here, the truth about power is told first to someone who lived under it. The shabad can be heard as grief, as protest, and as a sign that the Word would not stay silent.
screen: `AS THE WORD COMES, SO I SPEAK.` · `A WEDDING PARTY OF SIN FROM KABUL.` · `SONGS OF BLOOD, PLAINLY NAMED.` · `TOLD FIRST TO A WORKING FRIEND.` · then, large: `AS THE WORD COMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak honestly once. Sit and think of something true you've been holding back: at work, in your family, with a friend. Not a cruel truth, and not a rant. A true one, said with care. Notice whether you've been editing it to keep yourself safe. Now picture saying it plainly, as it comes, to the right person. Notice any fear, and what's underneath it. If you pray, you can ask the One for courage with a quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
As the Word comes to me. Guru Nanak to Bhai Lalo: as the Master's Word comes, so I speak, even about an invader's violence.
screen: `AS THE WORD COMES TO ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: as the word comes. Today, say one true thing you've been editing, kindly and plainly, to the person who needs to hear it. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

660.title: The one whose head He guards
660.word: The one whose head He guards
660.hook: the one who has You over his head, how can he suffer (Suhi M5, ang 749)
660.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Suhi shabad 'jis ke sir oopar toon suaamee' in kirtan, especially in hard times, and remember his martyrdom in 1606 each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, as the Word comes to me, and your line: as the word comes. What true thing did you say? Speaking that plainly takes courage. Today, where Guru Arjan says that courage comes from. Day six hundred sixty.

In Punjabi homes, when a child bends to touch a grandparent's feet, the grandparent often does one thing without thinking: they rest a hand on the child's head. A second, maybe two. It means: I bless you, I've got you, you're under my care. There's even an everyday phrase for having someone's hand on your head, meaning you have a protector, someone who stands behind you. Guru Arjan took that gesture and lifted it as high as it can go.
screen: `A CHILD TOUCHES AN ELDER'S FEET.` → `A HAND RESTS ON THE HEAD.` → `I'VE GOT YOU.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Raag Suhi, on ang 749. It begins, in effect: the one over whose head You stand, my Master, how could such a one suffer? Then it turns to the opposite person: someone drunk on the world's glitter doesn't know how to speak, and never remembers that he will die. Then the refrain: my Sovereign, You belong to Your devoted ones, and they belong to You. Your servant has no fear; even death's messenger doesn't come near. The word in the first line is sir, head. And in the gesture, as in the hymn, the head is where blessing lands and where protection is felt. Now, the honest question, the same one we asked about You are my father. Does this mean nothing bad ever happens to the faithful? Guru Arjan himself answers that, with his life. In 1606 he was arrested by the Mughal authorities in Lahore and died in their custody, after suffering Sikhs remember with grief every year. He's honored as the first Sikh martyr. So the hymn can't mean his devoted ones never meet pain. Sikhs read it at a deeper level: the one under the Master's hand isn't crushed by suffering. Dukh, pain, can come, but it doesn't own them. The fear is gone, even when the danger isn't. Tradition remembers Guru Arjan in his last days repeating that the Lord's will is sweet. That's what a guarded head looks like: not a life without storms, but a person who stays steady inside one.
screen: `SIR: THE HEAD, WHERE BLESSING LANDS.` · `HOW COULD SUCH A ONE SUFFER?` · `GURU ARJAN, MARTYRED IN 1606.` · `PAIN COMES, BUT DOESN'T OWN THEM.` · then, large: `GUARDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your hand on your head. Gently, the way a grandparent would. Feel its weight, its warmth. Let your shoulders drop under it. Think of who has been that hand for you: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend. And if you pray, let it stand for the One's hand, and say Waheguru quietly. Then think of something you're afraid of right now. Hold the fear and the hand at the same time. Notice which one feels bigger. When you're ready, lower your hand and rest. The bell holds the time.
The one whose head He guards. Guru Arjan: the one with the Master's hand over their head may meet pain, but not fear.
screen: `THE ONE WHOSE HEAD HE GUARDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: guarded. Today, when fear rises, touch the top of your head for a second and say the word. Day six hundred sixty.

screen: `DAY 660 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FRIEND HAS COME HOME.`

661.title: The Friend has come home
661.hook: the Friend has come to my home; the True One brought us together (Suhi M1, ang 764)
661.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Suhi chhant 'ham ghar saajan aae' in kirtan, and it is sung at the Anand Karaj, the wedding, before the lavan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one whose head He guards, and your line: guarded. Did you touch your head when fear rose? Today, a hymn of arrival, sung at Sikh weddings. Day six hundred sixty-one.

The doorbell rings and you already know who it is. Maybe a brother back from deployment, a daughter home from her first semester, an old friend you haven't seen in ten years. You open the door and the whole house changes. The air feels different. Somebody starts cooking. Guru Nanak wrote a hymn for exactly that feeling, the instant the one you've waited for crosses the threshold. And it is sung on a wedding morning.
screen: `THE DOORBELL RINGS.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE CHANGES.` → `A HYMN FOR THE THRESHOLD.`

segments.voice: The hymn is a chhant, a longer song form, in Raag Suhi, on ang 764. It opens, in effect: the friend has come to my home; the True One has brought about this meeting. Then: the meeting came naturally, pleasing to the Lord's mind; I've found what my heart was set on. Night and day there is union, my mind is content, my home and temple are made beautiful. The unstruck music plays. The friend has come to my home. The word is saajan: friend, beloved, the dear one. The verb, aae, can be read as one honored friend or many friends, and the hymn holds both. On the surface, guests arriving for a celebration, the house filling up. Underneath, the Beloved, the One, arriving in the heart. Tradition links Raag Suhi with weddings, and this chhant is sung at Sikh weddings before the couple walks the lavan. You can see why. A family's home fills with friends. Two people are brought together, and the hymn says plainly who did it: the True One made the meeting. And beneath it all, Gurbani's image of the soul as a bride waiting for the Beloved to come home. Notice the order in the hymn: the arrival first, and then the house becomes beautiful. Not the other way around. In the hymn, the home doesn't have to be perfect before the friend comes. The coming makes it beautiful. Tomorrow, the first of those four wedding rounds.
screen: `SAAJAN: FRIEND, BELOVED.` · `THE TRUE ONE MADE THE MEETING.` · `SUNG AS A WEDDING BEGINS.` · `THE COMING MAKES THE HOUSE BEAUTIFUL.` · then, large: `THE FRIEND IS HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Picture your own front door. Picture someone you love walking through it: someone who's coming soon, or someone you wish would. See their face as the door opens. Notice what changes in the room. Let whatever gladness comes be as big as it wants. Then, if you pray, you can welcome the One the same way, with a quiet Waheguru, as if the One were the friend at the door. If you don't, simply rest in the welcome. The bell holds the time.
The Friend has come home. Guru Nanak's wedding chhant: the friend has come to my home, the True One made the meeting, and the house is made beautiful.
screen: `THE FRIEND HAS COME HOME — today's word`.

662.title: Lav 1
662.hook: the first round: take up the work of dharma and the Name (Suhi M4, ang 773)
662.howItsDone: At an Anand Karaj, the granthi reads each of Guru Ram Das's four laavan stanzas, then the ragis sing it while the couple walks clockwise around the Guru Granth Sahib; the first round speaks of dharma and the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Friend came to the house, and your line: the friend is home. Did you welcome someone through your door, or back into your day? Today the friend stays, because today a wedding begins. Day six hundred sixty-two.

It's early morning at a gurdwara, and the hall is full of bright clothes. The bride and groom sit side by side on the floor, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, with a long scarf joining them, his end on his shoulder, hers in her hand. The hall goes quiet as the granthi turns to the page. The couple doesn't write vows. The words that marry them are a Guru's, and they come in four rounds. Today, the first: lav one.
screen: `A MORNING WEDDING IN A GURDWARA.` → `NO VOWS OF THEIR OWN.` → `FOUR ROUNDS OF WORDS.`

segments.voice: The Sikh wedding is called the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. At its center are four stanzas by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, in Raag Suhi, on Ang seven seventy-three. Each stanza is a lav, a round, and together they're the laavan. The pattern is simple. The granthi reads the first stanza aloud. Then the ragis sing it, and while they sing, the couple stands and walks once around the Guru Granth Sahib, clockwise, the groom usually a step ahead, the bride holding her end of the scarf. They bow, sit, and the next stanza is read. Four readings, four songs, four walks. What does the first round say? In paraphrase: in the first round, the Lord sets out the work of the householder's life. Take the Guru's word as your scripture; hold to dharma, right living; remember the Name. Notice what's missing. The first lav doesn't talk about romance, or the families, or the future house. It talks about a way of life the two will now walk together. Sikh teachers often read the four rounds on two levels at once: a husband and wife beginning a shared life, and a soul beginning its journey toward God. Round one is where both journeys start: with ordinary duty, done with the Name in mind. Guru Ram Das wrote it as a householder himself, a married man with children. In Sikh teaching that matters: the spiritual life isn't found by running away from home, but walked right through it.
screen: `ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.` · `READ, THEN SUNG, THEN WALKED.` · `ROUND ONE: DUTY, THE WORD, THE NAME.` · `TWO JOURNEYS IN ONE WALK.` · then, large: `ROUND ONE: DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one slow circle. If you have room, stand and walk a small circle, around a chair, a table, or just a spot on the floor, clockwise, slowly, one full round. If you can't walk, trace a circle with your hand. As you go, think of one plain duty in your life, the dishes, a shift at work, a call to a parent, and let it be part of the circle, not an interruption to it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you finish the round. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Lav. A round: one of the four stanzas of the Sikh wedding, read, sung, and walked around the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: round one: dharma. Today, do one ordinary duty as if it were part of a ceremony, slowly and on purpose. Day six hundred sixty-two.

663.title: Lav 2
663.hook: the second round: the Guru leads you to the fearless One, and ego's filth is gone (Suhi M4, ang 773)
663.howItsDone: At the Anand Karaj, the second of Guru Ram Das's four laavan is read and then sung while the couple walks a second time around the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first lav, and your line: round one: dharma. Did you do one plain duty slowly, as if it were part of a ceremony? The couple has bowed and sat down. The granthi opens to the second stanza. Day six hundred sixty-three.

Will this last? Am I enough? What will his mother think? What if we turn into our parents? Questions like these can sit under a wedding day, fear dressed up in flowers. The photos never show them. Under the music, two people are stepping into something they can't fully see. So it's striking that the second round of the Sikh wedding, sung while the couple walks, is about fear, and about leaving it behind. Today: lav two.
screen: `WILL THIS LAST? AM I ENOUGH?` → `FEAR DRESSED IN FLOWERS.` → `A ROUND ABOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: The second stanza of Guru Ram Das's laavan, still on Ang seven seventy-three, says, in paraphrase: in the second round, the Lord leads you to meet the true Guru. The mind becomes nirbhau, fearless, in the fear of God, and the filth of ego is washed away. One finds the pure fear, nirmal bhau. Singing the Lord's praises, you see the Lord everywhere, and the unstruck music sounds within. Two kinds of fear meet in that stanza, and the difference matters. One is the fear that shrinks you: what will people say, will I fail, what if I'm left. The other, in Gurbani's language, is bhau, a reverent awe of God, like standing at the edge of an ocean. The stanza holds the two together: in the pure fear of God, the mind becomes fearless. The awe loosens the grip of the smaller fears. And that word for fearless, nirbhau, has come up on this path before: in the Mul Mantar, at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, it's said of God, the Fearless One. In round two, the same word describes the mind walking toward Him. Ego is the other thing round two names. Haumai, the I that wants to win the argument, keep score, be right. The stanza calls it filth, and says it's washed off. For a couple, that's practical: a marriage where both people stop keeping score is a different marriage. For a soul, it's the next step after duty: once you're walking the path, the path starts to clean you. Then a lovely detail. The stanza says the unstruck sound, the anahad, plays inside. A music no one is playing. Round two ends listening.
screen: `ROUND TWO: TO MEET THE TRUE GURU.` · `TWO FEARS: THE SMALL ONE AND AWE.` · `NIRBHAU: FEARLESS, LIKE THE ONE.` · `EGO WASHED OFF, MUSIC WITHIN.` · then, large: `ROUND TWO: FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one slow circle again. Stand if you can, and walk a small clockwise round, or trace one with your hand. This time bring along one small fear you're carrying today. Name it plainly. Halfway around, let your attention widen: to the room, the sky outside, how much bigger the world is than the fear. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you complete the round. Then sit, and listen to whatever sound is there. The bell holds the time.
Lav two. The second round of the Sikh wedding: led to the true Guru, awe of God replaces the small fears, ego's filth washes away, and an unstruck music plays within.
Your line: round two: fearless. Today, when a small fear shows up, notice it, and then notice something bigger and older than it. Day six hundred sixty-three.

664.title: Lav 3
664.hook: the third round: longing for the Lord, and detachment within (Suhi M4, ang 774)
664.howItsDone: At the Anand Karaj, the third of the four laavan is read and sung while the couple walks a third time around the Guru Granth Sahib, with the congregation joining the singing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lav 2, and your line: round two: fearless. When a small fear came, did you notice something bigger beside it? Two rounds walked, two to go. The couple sits again, and the third stanza is read. Day six hundred sixty-four.

There's a kind of missing that happens even when someone is already yours. Two people in the same house, and one still looks up when the other walks in. A work trip, and the hotel bed feels too wide. It isn't loneliness exactly. It's longing that lives right next to love, and keeps it awake. Punjabi folk songs know it well: the bride waiting at the window, the lover across the river. The third round of the Sikh wedding takes that feeling and points it somewhere surprising. Today: lav three.
screen: `MISSING SOMEONE YOU HAVE.` → `LONGING THAT KEEPS LOVE AWAKE.` → `POINTED SOMEWHERE SURPRISING.`

segments.voice: The third stanza of the laavan, on Ang seven seventy-four, says, in paraphrase: in the third round, the mind fills with a longing for the Lord, and becomes detached. Meeting the holy company, by good fortune, one finds the Lord. One speaks the unspoken word, sings the Lord's praises, and the heart is lit with love. The key word is bairaag. It's usually translated detachment, and that sounds cold. But in this stanza bairaag is warm. It's the ache of separation, the yearning of someone who has glimpsed the Beloved and can't settle for less. The stanza says the mind becomes chaao, eager, and bairaagee, longing. Eager and longing in the same breath. So the detachment here isn't pulling away from the person beside you. It's that nothing small can be the center anymore: not status, not the guest list, not who was right last week. Longing for God loosens the grip of all of that. Notice, too, where the longing is found: in the sangat, the holy company. Round three isn't walked alone. That's true of a Sikh wedding literally: the whole congregation is there, singing. And it's true of a marriage: from the first round, a couple is surrounded by people who share what they care about. For the soul's journey, round three is the turn from discipline to desire. Round one was duty. Round two washed away fear and ego. In the soul's reading, round three is when the soul starts to want God, the way someone wants a person they love.
screen: `ROUND THREE: LONGING FOR THE LORD.` · `BAIRAAG: THE WARM ACHE.` · `FOUND IN THE HOLY COMPANY.` · `FROM DUTY TO DESIRE.` · then, large: `ROUND THREE: LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one slow circle, the third. Stand if you can and walk a small round clockwise, or trace one with your hand. As you walk, let yourself feel something you long for, not a thing to buy, but something deeper: peace, closeness, a sense of home. Don't fix it or explain it. Let the longing be there, warm, as you finish the round. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let the longing be the prayer. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Lav three. The third round of the Sikh wedding: the mind eager and longing, found in the holy company, lit with love for the Lord.
Your line: round three: longing. Today, when you miss someone, let it remind you what you most deeply want. Day six hundred sixty-four.

665.title: Lav 4
665.hook: the fourth round: the mind at peace, the Lord found in ease (Suhi M4, ang 774)
665.howItsDone: At the Anand Karaj, the fourth lav is read and sung as the couple walks a last time around the Guru Granth Sahib; the ceremony then closes with verses of Anand Sahib, Ardas and karah prashad.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lav 3, and your line: round three: longing. It closes a week that spoke as the Word came, rested under the Guru's guarding hand, welcomed the Friend home, and then walked a wedding: dharma, fearless, longing. One round left. Day six hundred sixty-five.

segments.voice: Picture a couple fifty years in. They're at the kitchen table doing the crossword. Nobody's talking much. One reaches for the pen and the other has already slid it across. There's nothing romantic about it, and yet it says more than a candlelit dinner could. Ease. Not the fireworks at the start, but a quiet that only comes after a long road. The last round of the Sikh wedding ends there, in a word that means exactly that kind of ease. Today: lav four.
screen: `FIFTY YEARS IN, A CROSSWORD.` → `THE PEN ALREADY SLID ACROSS.` → `A QUIET AFTER A LONG ROAD.`

segments.voice: The fourth stanza of Guru Ram Das's laavan, on Ang seven seventy-four, says, in paraphrase: in the fourth round, the mind becomes calm, and the Lord is found. The Lord is met in sahaj, in natural ease, and feels sweet to body and mind. The bride's heart blooms; she is joined with the Lord. And the stanza ends: in the fourth round, Nanak says, the eternal Lord is found. The word to hold is sahaj. It means ease, balance, the natural state. Gurbani uses it again and again for the settled peace of someone who has met God: not a high, but a level ground. So the four rounds trace a whole journey. Duty in round one. Fear and ego washed away in round two. Longing in round three. And in round four, rest. For the soul, that's union with God. For the couple, it's a picture of where a long marriage can arrive. Another line in the Guru Granth Sahib, by Guru Amar Das on Ang seven eighty-eight, says that husband and wife are not those who merely sit together; they are one light in two bodies. Many Sikhs think of that line at weddings. When the fourth round ends, the couple bows and sits, and the ceremony closes with the Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, and Ardas. Then the karah prashad is shared, and the two are married. No ring has to change hands. Four rounds of words, walked together, have done it.
screen: `ROUND FOUR: THE MIND AT REST.` · `SAHAJ: THE NATURAL EASE.` · `DUTY, FEARLESS, LONGING, REST.` · `ONE LIGHT IN TWO BODIES.` · then, large: `ROUND FOUR: UNION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk the last slow circle. Stand if you can and walk one small clockwise round, or trace it with your hand. This time, don't bring a duty or a fear or a longing. Just walk, at whatever pace is easy, and let your breath set the speed. When you finish, sit, and let yourself do nothing for a while. That's sahaj in miniature. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
Lav four. The last round of the Sikh wedding: the mind calm, the Lord met in natural ease, and the journey of the four rounds complete.
Your line: round four: union. Today, sit for a few minutes with someone you love and don't try to make it anything. Let it be easy. Day six hundred sixty-five.
